text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
JAMES CRICHTON, Scottish scholar who propounded many scientific theories and was known as "The Admirable Crichton," was born in 1560.
British poet JOHN DRYDEN was born in 1631.
Australian cattledog breeder THOMAS HALL was born in 1808. HALL's heelers were the first blue cattledogs - part dingo and part merle (a crossbred Scottish collie and Italian greyhound).
Australian cricketer THOMAS WILLS, who introduced Australian Rules Football as winter training for cricketers, was born in 1835.
American aviation pioneer ORVILLE WRIGHT was born in 1871. With his brother WILBUR, he made the first powered and controlled flight.
French fashion designer COCO CHANEL was born in 1883. She revolutionised women's clothing.
American humorist OGDEN NASH was born in 1902.
American jockey WILLY SHOEMAKER was born in 1931. He rode a record-breaking seven-thousand winners.
American singer JOHNNY NASH, who had a hit with "I Can See Clearly Now" in 1972, was born in 1940. By the age of 13 he was regularly singing in radio shows and on television.
British bass player and songwriter with 'Queen', JOHN DEACON, was born in 1951.
** EVENTS **
14 AD : The first Roman Emperor AUGUSTUS died.
1868 : The great eclipse cast a shadow across the earth.
The shadow swept across the Straits of Bab-el-Mandel to the Two Indian peninsulas, over Borneo and touched the northern extremity of Australia.
1904 : More than 40,000 people died from cholera in
Persia.
1930 : The major engineering feat of the Sydney Harbour
bridge was achieved with the joining of the north and south arches. It took five years to reach this stage. It would be another two years before the roadway would be opened to the public.
1934 : The German people voted overwhelmingly in favour

of ADOLF HITLER assuming the titles of "Fuhrer" and "Reich Chancellor". Thirty-eight million people voted 'yes' to giving HITLER the increased powers of combining the office of president and chancellor. About four-and-a-half million voted "No".
1936 : FEDERICO GARCIA LORCA, leading Spanish writer and
poet, was shot dead by Fascists at the beginning of the civil war.
1942 : British and Canadian troops launched a disastrous
attack on German-held Dieppe. Of the 6,000 troops involved, only about 2,500 returned; the rest were killed or captured.
1946 : More than three thousand people were killed in
riots between Moslems and Hindus in Calcutta. The unrest began over a British plan for India's constitution. The Moslem minority was seeking two separate nations.
1960 : The Soviets sentenced U-2 spy plane pilot GARY

POWERS to 10 years detention. POWERS was shot down near a Soviet armaments centre in the Urals three months earlier. He pleaded guilty to spying, and during his three day trial he apologised, saying he was acting under orders from the CIA. The flight led to the collapse of the summit in Paris between U.S. President
EISENHOWER and Premier KHRUSHCHEV, and cancellation of the president's planned visit to the Soviet Union.
1961 : The ABC'S "Four Corners" television programme was
screened for the first time.
1977 : GROUCHO MARX, the wise-cracking comic who made his

name by creating havoc on stage and in films, died of pneumonia. He was 81. His trademarks were his moustache, huge cigar and stooping walk. Brothers CHICO, HARPO, GUMMO, ZEPPO and GROUCHO began their film career in 1929 after success on Broadway.
1979 : The Vietnamese-backed Cambodian government passed

a death sentence on former dictator POL POT for genocide. The sentencing was passed in POL POT's absence, as government forces had been unable to track down the Khmer Rouge leader. During his reign of terror between 1975 and 1979 POL POT committed atrocities against the civilian population.
1987 : A lone gunman went on a six-hour rampage through

the small British town of Hungerford, killing 14 people including his mother. Another 14 were wounded. Ex-paratrooper, 27-year-old MICHAEL RYAN, shot himself after his killing spree. RYAN was said to have been deeply depressed by the death of his father, two years earlier.
1989 : Poland became the first Eastern European country
to end one-party rule, as Solidarity's TADEUZ MAZOWIECKI took office as prime minister.
1990 : Iraqi leader SADDAM HUSSEIN offered to release all
Western hostages in exchange for a US withdrawal from the Gulf region, and an end to the blockade.
1991 : Soviet leader MIKHAIL GORBACHEV was the subject of

a coup. The Tass news agency announced that the 60-year-old GORBACHEV was ill and unable to run the country. An "emergency committee" was formed to govern. GORBACHEV returned to Moscow two days later to retake control. The failed coup marked the beginning of the end of the old Soviet empire.
